about: Professional Skills in Civil Engineering (CEGE0102) is a Year 1 module in UCL's Civil Engineering programme and, according to the 2026/27 catalogue entry for CEGE0088, a prerequisite (with Civil Engineering Design, CEGE0003) for the Year 2 module Design and Professional Skills II. We could not read the module's own catalogue entry, so its credits, term, syllabus and assessment are not confirmed here. This is a guide pack: it explains what is known, gives background on professional formation and ethics, and offers general preparation for professional skills coursework, without inventing a syllabus.
topics: What this module is and what is confirmed
Professional formation: institutions, registration and ethics

notes.h: What Professional Skills in Civil Engineering is
notes.body:
Professional Skills in Civil Engineering (CEGE0102) is a first-year module on UCL's Civil Engineering degrees. Its CEGE code indicates the Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering.

What we could confirm from official UCL pages:
- UCL's 2026/27 catalogue entry for CEGE0088 names this module by code and title and calls it a Year 1 module.
- It is a prerequisite for the second-year module Design and Professional Skills II (CEGE0088), together with Civil Engineering Design (CEGE0003), according to the 2026/27 catalogue entry for CEGE0088. So this is the first-year foundation of a professional-skills strand that continues into Year 2.
- The 2026/27 description of CEGE0088 says it builds on the Year 1 modules and covers civil engineering design, project risk, legal aspects of civil engineering, health and safety, costing and tendering, through a term-long group design project. That tells you the direction the strand is heading, but it is not a description of CEGE0102 itself.
- UCL's Civil Engineering MEng page (for 2026 entry) describes Year 1 as building a theoretical foundation applied through Engineering Scenarios and Challenges, two interdisciplinary group projects, and a residential field trip to Wales covering surveying, dam design and environmental impact assessment. The page does not say which module each activity belongs to.

What we could not confirm:
- The catalogue entry for CEGE0102 itself could not be read when this pack was written, so we have not confirmed its credits, teaching term, syllabus, learning outcomes or assessment. This pack therefore does not set out a syllabus for it.
- Check the current catalogue entry and the module's Moodle page for the official description, the assessment components and deadlines.

How to use this pack:
- The next note gives background on professional formation (the institutions, registration and ethics) that underpins any professional skills teaching in an accredited engineering degree.
- The final note gives general advice on the kinds of coursework professional skills modules commonly involve (technical writing, calculations, drawings, teamwork and presentations). Treat it as preparation, and follow your module's own briefs where they differ.
- The related pack for Civil Engineering Design (CEGE0003) covers design process, CDM 2015, codes and teamwork in more depth; much of it is relevant here too.

notes.h: Professional formation: institutions, registration and ethics
notes.body:
Professional skills teaching in a civil engineering degree is aimed at your future registration as a professional engineer. It helps to know how the system works.

The bodies involved:
- The Engineering Council is the UK regulatory body for the engineering profession. It holds the national registers of Chartered Engineers (CEng), Incorporated Engineers (IEng), Engineering Technicians (EngTech) and ICT Technicians (ICTTech).
- It sets the standards for registration in UK-SPEC, its standard of professional engineering competence and commitment, which describes the competences and commitment expected at each level.
- Individuals register through professional engineering institutions licensed by the Engineering Council. For civil engineers the main ones are the Institution of Civil Engineers (ICE) and, for structural engineers, the Institution of Structural Engineers (IStructE).
- Degree programmes can be accredited as meeting the educational requirements for registration. Under Engineering Council rules, an accredited MEng provides the full educational base for CEng, while an accredited bachelor's (honours) degree meets the educational requirement for IEng and partly meets it for CEng, which then needs further learning, for example an accredited master's degree. Check UCL's programme page for your degree's current accreditation.

The route to chartership (in outline):
- Academic base (your degree).
- Initial professional development at work, often through a structured training scheme, building evidence against the institution's attributes or competences.
- A professional review (interview and written submission) by the institution.
- After registration, continuing professional development (CPD) throughout your career.
- Student membership of the ICE lets you use its resources and attend events now; ask about it through the department.

Ethics:
- The Engineering Council and the Royal Academy of Engineering publish a Statement of Ethical Principles. The 2017 edition has four principles: honesty and integrity; respect for life, law, the environment and public good; accuracy and rigour; and leadership and communication. Check the current version, as it is periodically reviewed.
- Institutions have their own codes or rules of professional conduct for members, and breaching them can lead to disciplinary action.
- In practice, ethics means things such as: only taking on work you are competent to do; being honest about uncertainty and errors; raising safety concerns rather than ignoring them; respecting confidentiality; avoiding conflicts of interest; and considering the environment and the wider public, not just the client.

Health and safety as a professional duty: in Great Britain, designers have legal duties under the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 to eliminate, reduce or control foreseeable risks so far as reasonably practicable (regulation 9). The second-year module in this strand covers health and safety, risk and legal aspects explicitly.

Why it matters now: habits of rigour (checking your calculations, stating assumptions, referencing sources honestly) are professional skills from day one, and academic integrity at university is the first test of the honesty principle.

We could not confirm how CEGE0102 is assessed, so this note covers skills that first-year professional skills teaching in engineering commonly develops, and that are useful across your Year 1 projects. Always follow the module's own briefs, templates and marking criteria.

Technical writing:
- Know your reader (client, checker, assessor) and write so they can act on it.
- A standard technical report structure: title page, summary (the key findings in a paragraph), introduction (purpose and scope), method, results, discussion, conclusions and recommendations, references, appendices.
- Put conclusions first in the summary; do not make the reader search for them.
- Short sentences, active voice where possible, consistent terminology, and units with every number.
- Number figures and tables, give them captions, and refer to each in the text.
- Proofread, and check that numbers in the text match the figures and appendices.

Referencing and academic integrity:
- Cite every source you use (data, figures, ideas) in the referencing style your department specifies, and list them at the end.
- Paraphrase in your own words and quote sparingly with quotation marks.
- Follow UCL's rules on academic integrity and on the use of AI tools for each assessment; they can differ between assessments.

Calculations:
- Set out calculations so a checker can follow them: state the problem, assumptions, sources of data (e.g. which code and clause), formulae, substitution, result with units, and a sentence saying what it means.
- Do a rough independent check (an order-of-magnitude estimate or equilibrium check).

Drawings and sketches:
- Clear titles, scales, north points on site plans, dimensions in consistent units (usually millimetres on engineering drawings), and labelled sections.
- A neat, annotated hand sketch often communicates a concept better than a rushed CAD drawing.

Data, spreadsheets and software:
- Label inputs, keep calculations transparent (no hard-typed numbers buried in formulae), and check spreadsheets with a hand calculation.
- If you use software such as CAD or GIS, keep source files organised and record data sources and any copyright or licence statements required.

Teamwork and presentations:
- Agree roles, a plan with deadlines and a single shared folder with version control; minute meetings with actions and owners.
- For presentations: one main message per slide, readable figures, rehearse timing, and prepare for questions.

Reflection: professional development relies on reflecting on what went well and what to improve. Record specific examples as you go; they are hard to remember later and are exactly what professional reviews ask for.

cards.b: The UK regulatory body for the engineering profession; holds the registers of CEng, IEng, EngTech and ICTTech and sets the UK-SPEC standard.
The Engineering Council's standard of professional engineering competence and commitment, setting what is required for CEng, IEng and EngTech.
Accredited degree (or equivalent), initial professional development at work, professional review by an institution, then CPD throughout your career.

cards.f: Accredited MEng vs accredited BEng for CEng
cards.b: An accredited MEng gives the full educational base for CEng; an accredited honours bachelor's degree needs further learning (e.g. an accredited master's).

cards.f: Four principles of the Statement of Ethical Principles (2017)
cards.b: Honesty and integrity; respect for life, law, the environment and public good; accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication.
Continuing professional development: the ongoing learning registered engineers are expected to plan, carry out and record throughout their careers.
Eliminate foreseeable health and safety risks so far as reasonably practicable; if not possible, reduce or control them, and provide information about remaining risks.

questions.q: Which body holds the UK register of Chartered Engineers?
questions.why: The Engineering Council regulates the profession and holds the national registers, including CEng. The Institution of Civil Engineers is a licensed institution that assesses its members and registers them with the Engineering Council, but it does not hold the national register itself. The Royal Academy of Engineering is the national academy for engineering (and co-publisher of the ethics statement), not the registration body. The Health and Safety Executive regulates workplace health and safety, not professional registration.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four principles in the Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering's Statement of Ethical Principles (2017)?
options: Respect for life, law, the environment and public good
questions.why: Commercial competitiveness is a business aim, not an ethical principle, so it is the answer. Accuracy and rigour, honesty and integrity, and respect for life, law, the environment and public good are three of the four principles; the fourth is leadership and communication.
